cards.title: Diagnose whether to consolidate or segment paid campaigns
cards.summary: Five diagnostic questions about categories, margin spread, personas, regions and creative throughput determine how much ad account segmentation is commercially justified.
cards.use_when: Deciding account structure (how many campaigns/adsets and what each represents) for a store's paid social or paid search account before restructuring or scaling spend.
steps: Ask how many product categories exist. More categories with different goals usually means more segmentation; a single-product store needs little.

Ask how wide the margin spread is. If gross margin varies substantially by category, or grade-A/B/C inventory must be cleared at discount, separating those lines prevents spend flowing to compressed-margin sale items.

Ask whether personas genuinely do not overlap. A men's range and a women's range should be separated; when audit shows women's ads serving to men, targeting has been 'confused' and capital is wasted. Overlapping tweaks to the same person do not require separation.
Ask how many regions you sell in and whether you hold inventory or have revenue targets there. Segmented spend control requires separate campaigns per region.
Ask what your creative throughput is. Ten new ads a month supports minimal segmentation; hundreds or thousands supports a testing structure that includes spend-allocation adsets.

Apply two non-negotiables: data integrity (whatever you build must produce readable, actionable reporting you can run decision loops on) and commercial alignment (the structure must expose categories that need spend, low-margin lines that cannot support paid acquisition, and KPIs the business actually tracks).
caveats: There is no universal account structure; two brands at the same revenue and margin can correctly end up with very different structures.
Adding campaigns 'because spend went up' without a commercial reason breaks data integrity.

cards.title: Consolidation vs segmentation: the small-sample tradeoff
cards.summary: Splitting conversions across many campaigns shrinks the optimization signal each one gets, so consolidate at campaign level while allowing more freedom at adset level.
cards.use_when: Planning how many campaigns to run for a low-to-mid-spend store's paid social account.
steps: Treat campaign level as the layer where conversion data is least shared. If you generate ~100 conversions a month and split them across four campaigns, each sees ~25 and results typically get worse from small sample size.

Consolidate upward at the campaign level by default: fewer campaigns means each machine-learning system has more signal to find buyers. The source notes accounts often start performing better when they crack through roughly 100–200 conversions per month because there is finally enough signal.

Segment more freely at adset level: more data inherits down from the campaign, so adset-level consolidation or fragmentation moves performance less (source estimates roughly 5–10% efficiency swings), and is context dependent.

Weigh the countervailing benefit of segmentation: when you split, you choose where budget goes. When you consolidate, the platform chooses, and it tends to run a Pareto distribution (roughly 20% of ads take ~80% of spend), which can starve a large batch of new creative or leave you with no backup once a winning ad fatigues.

Use the source's heuristic on who should consolidate: for a junior/in-house first-year buyer, more consolidation is preferable because the platform will allocate budget better than they will; an experienced buyer can run more controlled segmentation to force spend toward testing and de-risk fatigue.
caveats: The 100–200 conversions/month figure is the source's stated heuristic, not a measured benchmark.
Extreme 'consolidate everything into one campaign, one adset' advice is described as a bad idea for ~90% of brands, though some can get away with it.

Flexible/multi-creative ad units should be avoided when they hide per-creative reporting, because you cannot tell which asset is driving performance. Verify current platform naming and behavior before implementing.

cards.title: Set campaign structure from unit economics and AOV first
cards.summary: Different unit economics, audiences, or very high AOV with tiny conversion volume each argue against a single consolidated campaign.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether a large multi-SKU store or a high-ticket store can run a fully consolidated cold campaign.
steps: Separate campaigns when gross margin differs by category or grade. If you put full-price and heavily discounted inventory ads in one campaign, spend tends to flow to the discount items, compressing contribution margin and pushing sale messaging into your whole funnel and customer base.

Separate campaigns when audiences do not overlap. Men's and women's ranges in one adset cause misdelivery; use the platform's gender breakdown to spot ads serving to the wrong gender before restructuring.

For high-AOV, low-volume accounts (source example: ~$10,000 average order value, roughly five orders a day), be wary of campaign-budget-optimization that distributes at adset level: with very few attributable conversions, the platform optimizes upstream on CTR/CPC and hold rates. The source argues CPC has very weak correlation with return except at extremes, so you may be optimizing toward a metric unrelated to revenue.
In that case consider manual adset-level budget control instead of a CBO, accepting that the resulting structure will look unusual compared with a normal account.

Audit for the furniture-style failure mode: a consolidated cold CBO where ~57% of spend went to a single dynamic product ad adset. It reported strong ROAS on platform attribution, but 7-day-click and incrementality reads both came in far lower, showing overspend into an ad type that underperformed on cold audiences.
caveats: Case numbers are illustrative examples from one audit, not expected results.
Verify which attribution windows and incrementality tools your platform currently exposes, as options change.

cards.title: Drop daily bid and budget micro-tweaking; invest the time in creative
cards.summary: The source argues daily bid/budget tweaks are low-leverage compared with producing better creative and better landing pages.
cards.use_when: Deciding how an operator or media buyer should spend their weekly paid-media working hours.
steps: Stop daily bid adjustments (cost caps, bid caps changed every day). This was described as effective four to five years ago but now moves a lower-leverage variable; the source's framing is opportunity cost — the same hour spent on creative could 'double or triple' an account versus squeezing maybe ~5% from bid tweaks.
Stop daily budget pacing for smaller accounts, especially changes made on the basis of a day or two of data; small sample sizes make those decisions noise-driven.
Do continue to invest in account structure and architecture that matches commercial objectives, since this determines what data you can read and act on.

Do test concepts via adset-level segmentation rather than interest targeting. The source strongly asserts interest targeting and lookalike audiences no longer work and should be removed, freeing test budget.
Redirect that test budget into landing-page split tests and CRO, which the source treats as a higher-value experiment than platform audience tweaks.
Keep controlling the share of spend directed to existing customers over time, as a deliberate retention/allocation decision rather than an accidental overlap with cold campaigns.
caveats: The 5% bid-tweak gain and the 'no longer works' claims about interest/lookalike targeting are the presenter's opinions and platform-era judgments; verify against your own account data and current platform capabilities.
Some accounts may still find narrow interest layers useful; treat this as a situational position, not a universal rule.

cards.title: When and why to run a scaling campaign
cards.summary: A separate scaling campaign exists only to squeeze extra daily spend out of creative that has already been maxed out in its original adset.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add a scaling campaign to a store's paid social account.
steps: Confirm you actually have a winning adset hitting target ROAS and other soft metrics. Without a proven winner there is no reason to add the complexity.
Scale the adset up in spend until ROAS drops below a profitable threshold, then pull back to the equilibrium daily spend where it still performs.

Take those maxed-out creatives and launch them into a separate scaling campaign; the source's expectation is roughly an extra 20% in daily spend through the same creative on a good day, propped up by the new campaign's ability to find more delivery.

Apply a minimum-size test before bothering: an ad spending $60/day yields only ~$10 extra daily spend, which is not worth the management effort — fix the offer, landing page, or find a concept that works instead. Ads spending around $400/day unlock roughly $80/day each; running this across ten high performers could add about $1,000/day, which the source considers worthwhile.
KPI the scaling campaign at campaign level (not per adset), since there is typically no adset segmentation inside it.
Keep exclusions on the scaling campaign so existing customers are not re-served, and avoid running new creative testing inside the scaling campaign.
Do not kill testing too early: read conversion data over a long enough window to be valid for your volume (see the test-duration card).
caveats: The 'extra ~20% daily spend' figure is the source's rough expectation, not a guaranteed outcome.
Verify current platform behavior for adjacent-campaign delivery before relying on it.

cards.title: Set adset budgets from target CPA, not the 50-conversion rule
cards.summary: Derive the total test budget from target CPA and the run duration from seasonality and time-to-purchase, instead of applying the generic 50-conversions-per-7-days guideline.
cards.use_when: Setting adset-level budgets for a small or mid-size store's cold testing structure.
steps: Take target cost per acquisition (e.g., $50) and multiply by three to get the spend threshold for deciding whether a concept lives; at three or more conversions keep running, at two let it spend a further increment and re-decide, at zero or one cut it.
If the client will accept it, the source prefers a five-times-CPA threshold (e.g., $250) to remove the yellow-light judgment and make a clean yes/no decision.

Choose duration from two constraints: daily seasonality (a test launched on a strong weekday will look artificially good) and time to purchase (buyers often need multiple impressions and a few days of warming before converting).

Default to roughly one week; compress to three to four days for larger, stable accounts with short purchase cycles, and extend to 10–14 days for tiny budgets, long purchase cycles and heavy weekly seasonality.
When a test is not hitting KPI, diagnose the creative, produce more concepts, and then wind the adset down or switch it off rather than leaving it running.
For this spend level, do not read performance on windows shorter than about five days, and raise budgets on winning adsets in roughly 20% daily increments.
A known mistake to avoid: applying the '50 conversions in 7 days per adset' rule at low volume, which back-propagates budgets far too large for the business.
caveats: The 3x and 5x CPA thresholds and the one-week default are source heuristics; adjust to your own volume, AOV and purchase latency.
Reading windows must be sized to actual conversion volume — a 3-day window is meaningless at a few conversions per day.

cards.title: Structure cold testing around concepts, not audiences
cards.summary: Define a concept as persona × angle × offer, hold it in an adset, and rotate ad types and creative underneath it so you can read which concept earns spend.
cards.use_when: Building the creative-testing layer of a store's paid social account, or diagnosing why testing never produces a scalable winner.
steps: Assemble a concept matrix: personas × angles × offers, then produce creative under each concept across flexible ad types.
Example (teeth whitening): persona coffee drinkers, angle 'whitening without sensitivity issues', offer the product, ad type UGC. Under that adset you can rotate unlimited ad types.

Second example: persona brides, angle 'get ready for your wedding in 14 days', offer a curated fast-turnaround bundle, ad type testimonial with before/after documentation. Same product, entirely different concept.
Put each concept in its own adset with three to five creatives; more is fine if your creative volume supports it.

When you make more creative for an existing concept: if the adset is not performing, add the new creative to it to try to revive it; if it is hitting KPI, do not touch it — launch the concept as an additional adset instead. The source's first rule of paid media buying is never touch something that is working.
Expect concentration: one concept often outshines the rest, so you can legitimately end up with many adsets servicing a single winning concept.
KPI the testing campaign at adset level against target CPA or target ROAS over a window justified by conversion volume.
Exclude existing customers from testing so repeat buyers do not make a concept look better than it is, and set attribution to 7-day click for consistent reads.
caveats: Verify current platform options for flexible/multi-asset ad units, as naming and behavior change over time.
A 7-day click setting is the source's recommendation for data integrity; reconcile with any incrementality measurement you also run.

cards.title: Build the sub-$50k/month 'generic' structure
cards.summary: At low spend, run a consolidation-first structure of testing, optional scaling, and optional existing-customer retargeting, with existing customers excluded from cold.
cards.use_when: Standing up a paid social account for a store spending under roughly $50k per month on ads.
steps: Create a dedicated testing campaign (CBO or ABO — decide per your control preference) with adsets organised by concept and three to five creatives each.
Keep it consolidated: low conversion volume means the account should not be heavily segmented; the goal is to gather signal while forcing spend through adsets to learn.
Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns so testing is not skewed by repeat buyers, and set attribution to 7-day click.
Add a scaling campaign only once you have adsets that hit target ROAS (the source's example target was a 5x return) — see the scaling card for the spend-size threshold that justifies it.

Optionally add an existing-customer retargeting campaign. Decide by repeat-purchase expectation: model it on retention dynamics (furniture with low repeat frequency likely needs none; consumables/subscription-style products may justify a small, tightly controlled spend).
For existing-customer retargeting, KPI on incremental ROAS via an attribution breakdown and keep frequency below about seven on a 30-day rolling period.

Check whether a dedicated website-visitor retargeting campaign is needed by using the audience-segment breakdown (new / engaged / existing) to see whether organic delivery already spends enough into engaged users; for the source, ~90% of accounts do not need a separate warm-audience campaign.
caveats: The structure is deliberately generic; a custom structure from the five diagnostic questions will be better.
The 5x target ROAS and '90%' figure are source examples/estimates, not benchmarks.
Ensure audience-segment reporting is enabled in advertiser settings to get the engaged/existing breakdown.

cards.title: Extend from sub-$50k to $50k–$250k with commercially justified campaigns
cards.summary: At higher spend, add campaigns only where a specific commercial objective (funnel, category, new arrivals, regional target) justifies the extra fragmentation.
cards.use_when: Adding campaigns as a store's paid social budget grows from the sub-$50k range to roughly $50k–$250k per month.
steps: Keep the retargeting campaign, still usually existing customers only; website-visitor retargeting is rarely needed because cold campaigns already deliver to warm users.
Expand cold into more adsets as creative volume grows, and consider two or three campaigns when a real reason exists.

Single-SKU CPG example: split campaigns by funnel because the ad creative, landing page and sometimes the page handle differ entirely — one funnel targeting older buyers with VSLs, native statics, testimonials from that demographic and TV-style ads cut to UGC; another repositioning the same product for a younger performance/wellbeing angle. This behaves almost like two businesses, so it earns two campaigns.

Fashion example: bolt on a new-arrivals campaign to drive sell-through, or a category campaign (e.g., pants) when LTV analysis shows that category delivers a higher first-purchase AOV and better repeat rates — in that case you can accept a higher cost-per-acquisition KPI because you are acquiring higher-quality customers.
Do not add campaigns merely because spend increased; every segmentation decision must preserve readability and produce data you can act on.
Recognise that the real skill at this level is continuous testing to find the ~20% of concepts that can carry very large monthly spend.
caveats: The single-SKU CPG and pants-category examples are illustrations, not universal prescriptions.
Confirm your own LTV/repeat-rate analysis before raising CPA tolerance for a category.

cards.title: Work around the platform's active-ad cap with pages, partnerships and regional pages
cards.summary: When creative volume hits the ad-per-page limit, use extra brand pages, whitelisting/partnership ads and country-specific pages instead of deleting ads.
cards.use_when: Running high creative volume for a large store and hitting the platform's cap on active ads on a page.
steps: Know the constraint: the source states Meta caps active ads per page at roughly 300–500, so brands launching heavily every week exhaust it quickly.

Option 1 — spin up duplicate brand pages differing only by a small detail (the source cites a brand with around 15 near-identical pages differentiated by logo color). The source says for an ecommerce brand they would simply do this without worrying about single-page consolidation.

Option 2 — whitelisting: create a third-party-looking page (e.g., a 'magazine' handle) and run the same or lightly advertorial-adapted ads through it, so the creative appears to come from an outside source rather than the brand.
Option 3 — partnership ads: run ads through an influencer's or creator's real handle; often requires paying them if they have a following and leverage.

Option 4 — regional pages: if you sell in multiple countries, campaigns are usually segmented by country and identical ads count against each country's cap; create country-specific brand pages so each gets its own cap.
Stack all four if you run a brand at scale, rather than switching off ads to stay under one page's cap.
caveats: Ad-cap numbers and the exact naming of features may change — verify the current platform interface.
Partnership and whitelisting ads carry creator negotiation and disclosure considerations not covered here.

cards.title: Segment the account by region only when there is a commercial reason
cards.summary: Region segmentation should follow inventory location, fulfilment source and revenue targets, not just geography.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to split campaigns by country or consolidate regions for a store selling internationally.
steps: Separate campaigns by region when you hold inventory or have revenue/sell-through targets in that market; only segmentation gives you control over spend distribution.

Consider pairing markets that behave predictably: the source treats Australia + New Zealand as a natural pairing because New Zealand orders typically settle at roughly 7–10% of spend without overspending and are usually fulfilled from an Australian warehouse.

Consolidate regions into one campaign when all stock is held in one market and revenue location does not change inventory risk — you simply need to sell the stock regardless of where the order ships from.
Check operational constraints before consolidating: if the UK site sits on a different subdomain and ads must drive to different URLs, you likely need separate campaigns.

Watch seasonality conflicts (source example: Australia is southern hemisphere, the UK northern, so seasonal product performance differs), which may still force region separation or category adsets per region.
When campaign-level region separation creates too many campaigns, move category segmentation down to the adset level instead of duplicating the whole structure per region.
caveats: The 7–10% New Zealand spend figure is the source's observation for that pairing, not a general rule.
Fulfilment costs and shipping times should be checked in your own data before treating a region as controllable without its own campaign.

cards.title: Use adset-level category segmentation instead of doubling campaigns
cards.summary: When you need category control but not full campaign duplication, hold categories at the adset level and keep one cold campaign per region.
cards.use_when: Restructuring a multi-category store's account where the brand needs category-level budget control but campaign count is already high.
steps: Option A: keep one cold campaign per region (e.g., Australia, UK) and create category adsets underneath (pants, tops, dresses), giving you budget control per category without duplicating the entire campaign tree.

Option B: consolidate all regions into the same campaigns if shipping is centralised and you have no inventory-holding risk or target in the overseas market; sell-through is the only objective that matters, so geography becomes irrelevant to the structure.
Choose Option A when the overseas market has a different destination URL, different seasons, or its own sell-through target.
Keep a DPA retargeting campaign aimed at engaged audiences (e.g., 90-day website visitors), which the source reports performs strongly in fashion.

Add an existing-customer retargeting campaign with two separate adsets: new arrivals and a DPA. Keeping them separate matters because consolidating them sends nearly all spend to the DPA and new arrivals never reach existing customers.
The source notes existing-customer targeting in fashion is more incremental than in most categories, which justifies the dedicated spend.
caveats: The strong DPA and fashion-incrementality claims are the presenter's experience within their client base, not a general benchmark.
Category adsets still need enough conversion volume to be readable; too many thin adsets recreates the small-sample problem.

cards.title: Segment or consolidate — a two-brand worked example
cards.summary: Two brands at the same revenue and margin can need opposite structures because SKU count, persona count and region complexity differ.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of a store's commercial complexity should be reflected in the paid account structure.
steps: Brand A (CPG, single product, ~$5m/year, ~70% gross margin, one persona 'busy moms', selling AU and US): run one consolidated cold campaign per region using concept-based creative testing at adset level, with most spend flowing to the single performing concept.

For Brand A, exclude existing customers from cold (in CPG, returning-customer revenue tends to overattribute into cold and inflate the frequency of what is really retargeting). Add a small existing-customer retargeting campaign, in the source's example around $20/day, purely to keep frequency below about seven per 30 days.
The source's own view: at that revenue level they would only sell in AU, though the brand chose to expand.

Brand B (fashion, ~50 SKUs, same revenue, lower gross margin, four personas, selling AU, NZ and UK): build category campaigns (pants, tops, dresses) because categories have different purchase orders, revenue goals and sell-through risk requiring discounting.
Consolidate AU and NZ into one campaign; for the UK either move category segmentation down to adset level within one UK campaign, or consolidate regions if all stock is held in Australia.
In fashion, add a DPA retargeting campaign to 90-day visitors and a two-adset existing-customer campaign (new arrivals + DPA) so new arrivals always reach the customer base.
caveats: The $20/day retargeting figure and the 70% CPG margin are example values, not targets.
The recommendation to sell in one region at $5m/year is the presenter's opinion, not a rule.

cards.title: Control existing-customer spend and frequency
cards.summary: Allocate a deliberate, low, frequency-capped budget to existing customers instead of letting cold campaigns accidentally retarget them.
cards.use_when: Setting retention spend and exclusions across a store's paid social acquisition campaigns.
steps: Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns as standard, particularly in consumables where returning-customer revenue will otherwise overattribute into cold and inflate frequency until cold effectively becomes retargeting.

Decide the size of a dedicated existing-customer budget from repeat-purchase expectations and category: consumables, supplements and subscription models with high repeat rates justify spend; low-frequency categories such as furniture generally do not.

Keep the existing-customer campaign small and controlled rather than broad; use frequency rather than last-click ROAS as the primary control measure, keeping it below roughly seven per 30-day rolling period in the source's usage.
Measure it on incremental ROAS via an attribution breakdown, because existing-customer conversions will be claimed by cold campaigns if they are not excluded.
In fashion specifically, keep new arrivals and dynamic product ads as separate adsets, because a merged adset will send nearly all spend to the DPA and never surface new products to existing buyers.
In multi-category fashion, control spend per category so each category hits sell-through and does not have to be discounted, protecting gross margin.
caveats: The frequency ceiling of ~7 per 30 days is the source's operating heuristic, not a universal threshold.
Platform attribution windows and incrementality reporting differ; verify current measurement options.

cards.title: Log these four account-level mistakes at low spend
cards.summary: Common low-spend errors: testing inside the scaling campaign, skipping exclusions, killing tests too early, and over-budgeting adsets via the 50-conversion rule.
cards.use_when: Auditing a small store's paid social account before restructuring or scaling.
steps: Check whether creative testing is running inside the scaling campaign; testing belongs in the dedicated testing campaign where you can read results per adset.
Check whether the scaling campaign has exclusions applied; without them, it re-serves existing and engaged audiences and distorts reads.
Check the length of time tests run before being switched off. Killing tests inside a few days ignores daily seasonality and time-to-purchase and produces biased conclusions.

Check whether adset budgets were set from the 50-conversions-in-7-days rule; at low volume this produces budgets far larger than the business can support. Back-propagate the budget from target CPA and AOV instead.
Check whether retargeting or scaling campaigns are running before there is any proven winning creative to scale; without a winner these add complexity without return.
Confirm data integrity: 7-day-click attribution, existing customers excluded from cold, and adset-level KPI reads on a window sized to conversion volume.
caveats: These are diagnostic checks, not a complete account audit checklist.
Attribution-setting advice should be confirmed against your current measurement setup and any incrementality testing you run.

Ads spending around $400/day unlock roughly $80/day each; running this across ten high performers could add about $1,000/day, which the source considers worthwhile.","KPI the scaling campaign at campaign level (not per adset), since there is typically no adset segmentation inside it.","Keep exclusions on the scaling campaign so existing customers are not re-served, and avoid running new creative testing inside the scaling campaign.","Do not kill testing too early: read conversion data over a long enough window to be valid for your volume (see the test-duration card)."],"caveats":["The 'extra ~20% daily spend' figure is the source's rough expectation, not a guaranteed outcome.","Verify current platform behavior for adjacent-campaign delivery before relying on it."],"tags":["multi","campaign-structure","performance-marketing","scaling","media-buying","measurement"]},{"title":"Set adset budgets from target CPA, not the 50-conversion rule","summary":"Derive the total test budget from target CPA and the run duration from seasonality and time-to-purchase, instead of applying the generic 50-conversions-per-7-days guideline.","use_when":"Setting adset-level budgets for a small or mid-size store's cold testing structure.","steps":["Take target cost per acquisition (e.g., $50) and multiply by three to get the spend threshold for deciding whether a concept lives; at three or more conversions keep running, at two let it spend a further increment and re-decide, at zero or one cut it.","If the client will accept it, the source prefers a five-times-CPA threshold (e.g., $250) to remove the yellow-light judgment and make a clean yes/no decision.","Choose duration from two constraints: daily seasonality (a test launched on a strong weekday will look artificially good) and time to purchase (buyers often need multiple impressions and a few days of warming before converting).","Default to roughly one week; compress to three to four days for larger, stable accounts with short purchase cycles, and extend to 10–14 days for tiny budgets, long purchase cycles and heavy weekly seasonality.","When a test is not hitting KPI, diagnose the creative, produce more concepts, and then wind the adset down or switch it off rather than leaving it running.","For this spend level, do not read performance on windows shorter than about five days, and raise budgets on winning adsets in roughly 20% daily increments.","A known mistake to avoid: applying the '50 conversions in 7 days per adset' rule at low volume, which back-propagates budgets far too large for the business."],"caveats":["The 3x and 5x CPA thresholds and the one-week default are source heuristics; adjust to your own volume, AOV and purchase latency.","Reading windows must be sized to actual conversion volume — a 3-day window is meaningless at a few conversions per day."],"tags":["multi","experiment-design","performance-marketing","budgeting","measurement","campaign-structure"]},{"title":"Structure cold testing around concepts, not audiences","summary":"Define a concept as persona × angle × offer, hold it in an adset, and rotate ad types and creative underneath it so you can read which concept earns spend.","use_when":"Building the creative-testing layer of a store's paid social account, or diagnosing why testing never produces a scalable winner.","steps":["Assemble a concept matrix: personas × angles × offers, then produce creative under each concept across flexible ad types.","Example (teeth whitening): persona coffee drinkers, angle 'whitening without sensitivity issues', offer the product, ad type UGC. Under that adset you can rotate unlimited ad types.","Second example: persona brides, angle 'get ready for your wedding in 14 days', offer a curated fast-turnaround bundle, ad type testimonial with before/after documentation. Same product, entirely different concept.","Put each concept in its own adset with three to five creatives; more is fine if your creative volume supports it.","When you make more creative for an existing concept: if the adset is not performing, add the new creative to it to try to revive it; if it is hitting KPI, do not touch it — launch the concept as an additional adset instead. The source's first rule of paid media buying is never touch something that is working.","Expect concentration: one concept often outshines the rest, so you can legitimately end up with many adsets servicing a single winning concept.","KPI the testing campaign at adset level against target CPA or target ROAS over a window justified by conversion volume.","Exclude existing customers from testing so repeat buyers do not make a concept look better than it is, and set attribution to 7-day click for consistent reads."],"caveats":["Verify current platform options for flexible/multi-asset ad units, as naming and behavior change over time.","A 7-day click setting is the source's recommendation for data integrity; reconcile with any incrementality measurement you also run."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","experiment-design","performance-marketing","product-page","acquisition","campaign-structure"]},{"title":"Build the sub-$50k/month 'generic' structure","summary":"At low spend, run a consolidation-first structure of testing, optional scaling, and optional existing-customer retargeting, with existing customers excluded from cold.","use_when":"Standing up a paid social account for a store spending under roughly $50k per month on ads.","steps":["Create a dedicated testing campaign (CBO or ABO — decide per your control preference) with adsets organised by concept and three to five creatives each.","Keep it consolidated: low conversion volume means the account should not be heavily segmented; the goal is to gather signal while forcing spend through adsets to learn.","Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns so testing is not skewed by repeat buyers, and set attribution to 7-day click.","Add a scaling campaign only once you have adsets that hit target ROAS (the source's example target was a 5x return) — see the scaling card for the spend-size threshold that justifies it.","Optionally add an existing-customer retargeting campaign. Decide by repeat-purchase expectation: model it on retention dynamics (furniture with low repeat frequency likely needs none; consumables/subscription-style products may justify a small, tightly controlled spend).","For existing-customer retargeting, KPI on incremental ROAS via an attribution breakdown and keep frequency below about seven on a 30-day rolling period.","Check whether a dedicated website-visitor retargeting campaign is needed by using the audience-segment breakdown (new / engaged / existing) to see whether organic delivery already spends enough into engaged users; for the source, ~90% of accounts do not need a separate warm-audience campaign."],"caveats":["The structure is deliberately generic; a custom structure from the five diagnostic questions will be better.","The 5x target ROAS and '90%' figure are source examples/estimates, not benchmarks.","Ensure audience-segment reporting is enabled in advertiser settings to get the engaged/existing breakdown."],"tags":["multi","campaign-structure","retention","performance-marketing","measurement","attribution","budgeting"]},{"title":"Extend from sub-$50k to $50k–$250k with commercially justified campaigns","summary":"At higher spend, add campaigns only where a specific commercial objective (funnel, category, new arrivals, regional target) justifies the extra fragmentation.","use_when":"Adding campaigns as a store's paid social budget grows from the sub-$50k range to roughly $50k–$250k per month.","steps":["Keep the retargeting campaign, still usually existing customers only; website-visitor retargeting is rarely needed because cold campaigns already deliver to warm users.","Expand cold into more adsets as creative volume grows, and consider two or three campaigns when a real reason exists.","Single-SKU CPG example: split campaigns by funnel because the ad creative, landing page and sometimes the page handle differ entirely — one funnel targeting older buyers with VSLs, native statics, testimonials from that demographic and TV-style ads cut to UGC; another repositioning the same product for a younger performance/wellbeing angle. This behaves almost like two businesses, so it earns two campaigns.","Fashion example: bolt on a new-arrivals campaign to drive sell-through, or a category campaign (e.g., pants) when LTV analysis shows that category delivers a higher first-purchase AOV and better repeat rates — in that case you can accept a higher cost-per-acquisition KPI because you are acquiring higher-quality customers.","Do not add campaigns merely because spend increased; every segmentation decision must preserve readability and produce data you can act on.","Recognise that the real skill at this level is continuous testing to find the ~20% of concepts that can carry very large monthly spend."],"caveats":["The single-SKU CPG and pants-category examples are illustrations, not universal prescriptions.","Confirm your own LTV/repeat-rate analysis before raising CPA tolerance for a category."],"tags":["multi","campaign-structure","performance-marketing","scaling","retention","creative-strategy","product-selection"]},{"title":"Work around the platform's active-ad cap with pages, partnerships and regional pages","summary":"When creative volume hits the ad-per-page limit, use extra brand pages, whitelisting/partnership ads and country-specific pages instead of deleting ads.","use_when":"Running high creative volume for a large store and hitting the platform's cap on active ads on a page.","steps":["Know the constraint: the source states Meta caps active ads per page at roughly 300–500, so brands launching heavily every week exhaust it quickly.","Option 1 — spin up duplicate brand pages differing only by a small detail (the source cites a brand with around 15 near-identical pages differentiated by logo color). The source says for an ecommerce brand they would simply do this without worrying about single-page consolidation.","Option 2 — whitelisting: create a third-party-looking page (e.g., a 'magazine' handle) and run the same or lightly advertorial-adapted ads through it, so the creative appears to come from an outside source rather than the brand.","Option 3 — partnership ads: run ads through an influencer's or creator's real handle; often requires paying them if they have a following and leverage.","Option 4 — regional pages: if you sell in multiple countries, campaigns are usually segmented by country and identical ads count against each country's cap; create country-specific brand pages so each gets its own cap.","Stack all four if you run a brand at scale, rather than switching off ads to stay under one page's cap."],"caveats":["Ad-cap numbers and the exact naming of features may change — verify the current platform interface.","Partnership and whitelisting ads carry creator negotiation and disclosure considerations not covered here."],"tags":["multi","creative-strategy","scaling","acquisition","performance-marketing","campaign-structure"]},{"title":"Segment the account by region only when there is a commercial reason","summary":"Region segmentation should follow inventory location, fulfilment source and revenue targets, not just geography.","use_when":"Deciding whether to split campaigns by country or consolidate regions for a store selling internationally.","steps":["Separate campaigns by region when you hold inventory or have revenue/sell-through targets in that market; only segmentation gives you control over spend distribution.","Consider pairing markets that behave predictably: the source treats Australia + New Zealand as a natural pairing because New Zealand orders typically settle at roughly 7–10% of spend without overspending and are usually fulfilled from an Australian warehouse.","Consolidate regions into one campaign when all stock is held in one market and revenue location does not change inventory risk — you simply need to sell the stock regardless of where the order ships from.","Check operational constraints before consolidating: if the UK site sits on a different subdomain and ads must drive to different URLs, you likely need separate campaigns.","Watch seasonality conflicts (source example: Australia is southern hemisphere, the UK northern, so seasonal product performance differs), which may still force region separation or category adsets per region.","When campaign-level region separation creates too many campaigns, move category segmentation down to the adset level instead of duplicating the whole structure per region."],"caveats":["The 7–10% New Zealand spend figure is the source's observation for that pairing, not a general rule.","Fulfilment costs and shipping times should be checked in your own data before treating a region as controllable without its own campaign."],"tags":["multi","campaign-structure","regional","fulfillment","inventory","performance-marketing"]},{"title":"Use adset-level category segmentation instead of doubling campaigns","summary":"When you need category control but not full campaign duplication, hold categories at the adset level and keep one cold campaign per region.","use_when":"Restructuring a multi-category store's account where the brand needs category-level budget control but campaign count is already high.","steps":["Option A: keep one cold campaign per region (e.g., Australia, UK) and create category adsets underneath (pants, tops, dresses), giving you budget control per category without duplicating the entire campaign tree.","Option B: consolidate all regions into the same campaigns if shipping is centralised and you have no inventory-holding risk or target in the overseas market; sell-through is the only objective that matters, so geography becomes irrelevant to the structure.","Choose Option A when the overseas market has a different destination URL, different seasons, or its own sell-through target.","Keep a DPA retargeting campaign aimed at engaged audiences (e.g., 90-day website visitors), which the source reports performs strongly in fashion.","Add an existing-customer retargeting campaign with two separate adsets: new arrivals and a DPA. Keeping them separate matters because consolidating them sends nearly all spend to the DPA and new arrivals never reach existing customers.","The source notes existing-customer targeting in fashion is more incremental than in most categories, which justifies the dedicated spend."],"caveats":["The strong DPA and fashion-incrementality claims are the presenter's experience within their client base, not a general benchmark.","Category adsets still need enough conversion volume to be readable; too many thin adsets recreates the small-sample problem."],"tags":["multi","campaign-structure","regional","retention","merchandising","performance-marketing","fashion"]},{"title":"Segment or consolidate — a two-brand worked example","summary":"Two brands at the same revenue and margin can need opposite structures because SKU count, persona count and region complexity differ.","use_when":"Deciding how much of a store's commercial complexity should be reflected in the paid account structure.","steps":["Brand A (CPG, single product, ~$5m/year, ~70% gross margin, one persona 'busy moms', selling AU and US): run one consolidated cold campaign per region using concept-based creative testing at adset level, with most spend flowing to the single performing concept.","For Brand A, exclude existing customers from cold (in CPG, returning-customer revenue tends to overattribute into cold and inflate the frequency of what is really retargeting). Add a small existing-customer retargeting campaign, in the source's example around $20/day, purely to keep frequency below about seven per 30 days.","The source's own view: at that revenue level they would only sell in AU, though the brand chose to expand.","Brand B (fashion, ~50 SKUs, same revenue, lower gross margin, four personas, selling AU, NZ and UK): build category campaigns (pants, tops, dresses) because categories have different purchase orders, revenue goals and sell-through risk requiring discounting.","Consolidate AU and NZ into one campaign; for the UK either move category segmentation down to adset level within one UK campaign, or consolidate regions if all stock is held in Australia.","In fashion, add a DPA retargeting campaign to 90-day visitors and a two-adset existing-customer campaign (new arrivals + DPA) so new arrivals always reach the customer base."],"caveats":["The $20/day retargeting figure and the 70% CPG margin are example values, not targets.","The recommendation to sell in one region at $5m/year is the presenter's opinion, not a rule."],"tags":["multi","campaign-structure","margin-analysis","retention","merchandising","performance-marketing","regional"]},{"title":"Control existing-customer spend and frequency","summary":"Allocate a deliberate, low, frequency-capped budget to existing customers instead of letting cold campaigns accidentally retarget them.","use_when":"Setting retention spend and exclusions across a store's paid social acquisition campaigns.","steps":["Exclude existing customers from cold campaigns as standard, particularly in consumables where returning-customer revenue will otherwise overattribute into cold and inflate frequency until cold effectively becomes retargeting.","Decide the size of a dedicated existing-customer budget from repeat-purchase expectations and category: consumables, supplements and subscription models with high repeat rates justify spend; low-frequency categories such as furniture generally do not.","Keep the existing-customer campaign small and controlled rather than broad; use frequency rather than last-click ROAS as the primary control measure, keeping it below roughly seven per 30-day rolling period in the source's usage.","Measure it on incremental ROAS via an attribution breakdown, because existing-customer conversions will be claimed by cold campaigns if they are not excluded.","In fashion specifically, keep new arrivals and dynamic product ads as separate adsets, because a merged adset will send nearly all spend to the DPA and never surface new products to existing buyers.","In multi-category fashion, control spend per category so each category hits sell-through and does not have to be discounted, protecting gross margin."],"caveats":["The frequency ceiling of ~7 per 30 days is the source's operating heuristic, not a universal threshold.","Platform attribution windows and incrementality reporting differ; verify current measurement options."],"tags":["multi","retention","attribution","frequency","margin-analysis","performance-marketing","merchandising"]},{"title":"Log these four account-level mistakes at low spend","summary":"Common low-spend errors: testing inside the scaling campaign, skipping exclusions, killing tests too early, and over-budgeting adsets via the 50-conversion rule.","use_when":"Auditing a small store's paid social account before restructuring or scaling.","steps":["Check whether creative testing is running inside the scaling campaign; testing belongs in the dedicated testing campaign where you can read results per adset.","Check whether the scaling campaign has exclusions applied; without them, it re-serves existing and engaged audiences and distorts reads.","Check the length of time tests run before being switched off. Killing tests inside a few days ignores daily seasonality and time-to-purchase and produces biased conclusions.","Check whether adset budgets were set from the 50-conversions-in-7-days rule; at low volume this produces budgets far larger than the business can support. Back-propagate the budget from target CPA and AOV instead.","Check whether retargeting or scaling campaigns are running before there is any proven winning creative to scale; without a winner these add complexity without return.","Confirm data integrity: 7-day-click attribution, existing customers excluded from cold, and adset-level KPI reads on a window sized to conversion volume."],"caveats":["These are diagnostic checks, not a complete account audit checklist.","Attribution-setting advice should be confirmed against your current measurement setup and any incrementality testing you run."],"tags":["multi","performance-marketing","measurement","attribution","experiment-design","campaign-structure","audit"]}]}

And it's because you do need a level of segmentation within the account to better commercially align with the objectives of most businesses. The reason why campaign segmentation exists, the reason why you can make multiple campaigns is because businesses often need to flow budgets through different campaigns over time. And so you might have a promotion that rolls in that then rolls into something else. And so you need segmentation in the actual KPIing and reporting. Number one. Number two is different business units exist in a lot of businesses, which is that you might have a category for pets and then you have a category for children. As a product of that, you don't want the campaign getting confused and not understanding who to target when you have slightly different demographics. And so, as a product of that, you want the ability to be able to segment the account based on the actual segmentation of personas within the business. And this allows you to do it. And one of the downsides of that is that conversion data here is not shared at the same level as it is at the adset and ad level.

 And so is there some conversion data sharing going on here? For sure. Campaign one is pulling from some of the signals of campaign 2 and vice versa. But they're not directly sharing all of the conversion data with each other. Which means that if you start to introduce a bunch of campaigns in the account and you have let's say four campaigns for a small ad account with not much budget, what you're actually doing is taking all your conversion data. Let's say you're getting 100 conversions a month and you're splitting it up across four campaigns. So now you have 25 25. You're inherently going to get worse results in the account due to segmentation because now you have less conversion data that these campaigns can optimize on. And anytime you have less conversion data, you will see worse results due to small sample size bite. Which simply means that if you don't have a lot of conversions, meta doesn't have a lot of signal and so it doesn't really know who to touch. The more signal you have, the more conversions you have, generally actually the better the efficiency is. Which is why you often actually see that when you can crack through 100 or 200 conversions a month, the ad account starts performing better rather than worse. And it's because there's enough signal that Meta now understands who to target properly. And you can get out of that rut of Meta not really understanding who to target because there's not enough conversion data. So you always generally want to be consolidating up at the campaign level cuz every time you segment, you're chunking out the data. Same thing kind of applies at the adset level, not as much. There is more data sharing that occurs here than at the campaign level. Number one. Number two is that all the data at the campaign level also inherits down. So you don't really have to worry as much about segmentation at the adset level. You can kind of segment all you want. It's not going to impact performance that heavily. You can consolidate up. It's not going to perform impact performance that heavily. We're talking about really 5 to 10% efficiency swings here based on hyper segmentation versus consolidation. It's noticeable particularly at scale, but it's also going to be context dependent on the actual. Then at the ad level, obviously you're going to have massive segmentation because you can't stack ad. Now you technically can stack ads and the name of this always changes. So by the time you're watching this, it might be different. At the moment, it's called flexible ads, which is where you can load in like five different creative on the same ad. The reason why we generally don't like these is because you don't get visibility into data insights. And so you can go and load five creative up into one ad, which is all well and good. Nice. It's consolidated. Meta prefers consolidation. So it seems like the right idea. But the issue is when this ad performs well, we don't know what creative is actually performing well. Is it creative one, two, three, four, five? which of the creative that we put in here is actually lifting performance because we want to do more like that. We want to make more ads like that. But if we don't have the ability to read the insight, well, it's kind of useless. Yeah, we got performance, but now we don't know what to do with it. There's also a couple other benefits of consolidation over segmentation. And this is mainly letting the machine decide where to distribute spend. Now, this can be a bad thing and it can overweight your account into a heavy degree of risk, but can be a good thing if you're just trying to maximize efficiency in the short term, which is that when we're talking about consolidation, Meta is picking where to distribute your spend. If you just have everything sitting in a campaign that's a CVO with a bunch of adsets with a bunch of ads, Meta is just going to go and swing budgets around based on what it believes is most efficient. when you have segmentation and let's say an structure. So you're choosing where budgets go at the adset level. Well, you are deciding where the budget goes and inherently meta will always in most cases distribute budget more efficiently than you will. However, Meta will also therefore distribute budget on an 80/20 Purto sprint, which is 20% of your ads will get 80% of the spend. Now, kind of annoying if you're making a 100 new ads a month and none of them are getting any spend and they're not getting tested. Also kind of annoying if all the spend goes into just one creative and maybe you're paying influencers for partnership ads that are getting no spend or maybe you know that creative is going to fatigue and now you're like we're in a risky position because we have no backup ads that are doing well. And so this can be good but it can also hurt you. Whereas on segmentation you're going to be forcing spend across a structure in a way that you want which technically might derisk you might put you in a better position might facilitate better testing. uh if you're a novice and you're not doing this thoughtfully and methodically and carefully, well then you can just end up burning a bunch of money here. And so a good way to kind of think through this problem is that if let's say you're an in-house business, $10 million a year and you're making an in-house media buying hire. If you're hiring someone that is in their first year and they have kind of no idea what they're doing, I would prefer they run this structure cuz I would actually prefer Meta Distributes budgets over them because they don't know what they're doing. If you know what you're doing and you're experienced and you understand weighing risk against profit and efficiency and understanding the changes that need to be made, I would much prefer they run this structure or somewhere in the middle so that we can still have control over where spend's getting forced carefully and thoughtfully, but we're not just burning money. There's also the extreme of this which is there is a circle on the internet that is focused around consolidate everything. Just run one campaign, one ad set, throw all the ads under it. That's all you need. You don't need an agency. You don't need any kind of media buying. You don't need any kind of segmentation. You don't need structure. Just consolidate. Just upload ads into a campaign and you're good. That's a terrible idea for 90% of people. Now, 10% of brands can get away with that and they'll be okay. But there's three reasons as to why you don't want to just consolidate everything. Number one is different unit economics. And so, if you're a large business with a lot of SKs, generally the unit economics or the gross margin will change across different categories. you will have 70% gross margin on this particular product range. But on this particular product range, maybe you have 60%. Or you will have grade A, grade B, grade C, grade D inventory. So on your grade A inventory, you have incredible unit. On your grade C inventory, you also have incredible unit. Your gross margin is the same. It's great, but it's not selling. And so because of that, you generally have to discount it hard, which compresses the actual margin post discount. And so if we put both of those products or both of those ads into the one campaign, we would end up with likely a lot of spend getting distributed to the heavy sale items. But the heavy sale items is not where we want our budget to go because we have compressed margin there. We're probably going to end up with worse contribution margin and it's also just bad branding to be heavy pushing sales messaging through our entire funnel and existing customers. So when you have different unit economics across the product portfolio, you actually want segmentation. Number two is you might have different audiences. And so an easy example of this means that you might have an activewear brand and the activewear brand sells to both men and women. Now if you go and put all the men and all the women ads into one adset into one campaign, the adset is likely going to get confused. And in fact, you see this on ad accounts all the time. This is an easy call out anytime I audit a brand that sells to both men and women through core different product ranges. So there's a men's range and there's a women's range is that you just go down under the adset level and you just take a look at all the ads. You use the breakdown feature. you look at gender split and what you'll end up seeing is that women ads are going to men and men ads are going to women. Now men ads serving to women isn't as bad of a idea because women do a lot of purchasing for their partners and so you end up seeing directional purchase behavior from women to men but you don't see it as much in the other direction dependent on the category and so you generally don't want to be pushing women's active wear ads to men. Will you get a return? Sure. People will buy. You still get a return on it. Is it the most efficient use of your capital in the business? Absolutely not. You should serve your women's active wear ads to women. And so if you just go and put all of these in the one ad set because targeting primarily exists at the adset level, that is where you choose the targeting. That is where the targeting generally resides for most of what's occurring under it. It gets confused. It doesn't know where to serve them. So, it's just serving them to everyone. Number three is high average order value or low conversion volume accounts. We have some clients that we work with where average order value is $10,000. on a $10,000 average order value. The issue is is that you just don't do much order volume. And so this brand as an example, I think they do 50k a day or something like that, it's only five orders a day. Not a lot of purchase volume at all. And so what ends up happening in an account like this is that if you have a CBO as an example, and this is a bunch of ad sets, so this is ad set one, set two, etc., is that Meta will distribute budget at the adset level not based on purchase, not based on row, not based on actual signal that we care about. Instead, because there's nowhere near enough signal, there's only like five conversions max getting attributed into the account per day. What ends up happening is Meta needs to go upstream in its optimization. And so, it goes up and starts looking at CTRs and CPCs and hold rates. And now sure these are pre-intent pre-click signals as to something that might infer future performance. But unfortunately the reality is when you look at very large data sets CPCs are not correlated with returns except for the extremity of bounds. And so if CPCs are super high yes ROI will be super low. If CPCs are super high that actually doesn't correlate with ROI. So what you end up saying when you graph this out is you just say something like this, which is that cost per click has almost no correlation or a very weak correlation to actual return on the ad. And so if we're optimizing budget distribution based on cost per click or CTR, we're optimizing it towards a metric that has nothing really to do with the actual core objective, which is to drive revenue. And so in this case, we likely don't want to use a CBO. We likely don't want the campaign to distribute budgets how it is. And we want to think through a structure that's going to look very different from what you would expect in any other account which is sort of getting us towards the position of every account looks different depending on the actual commercial objectives of the business. What do the unit economics look like? What do the audience profiles and personas look like? What does the average order value and conversion volume look like? Because all of these things will change how we approach consolidation or segmentation. I'll give you a tactical example of where consolidation on an audit I did a few weeks ago was very relevant and not a good idea which was this was a furniture brand about 20 to 30 million they had a cold campaign which was consolidated that's all they had and then it was a CBO and they had a bunch of adsets down here now the issue was 57% of the meta budget was going into the top adset now what was this adset it was just a dynamic product app now the issue is return on ad spend looks really good on service it was like a seven rorowaz but once you break down to 7-day click or you break down to incremental attribution either one gave the same read returns was actually a 1.9 everything else was performing better than this on an incremental or a 7-day click rate and so this was a good example of where them just consolidating up and putting DPAs in with everything else not a good idea particularly in that industry because you'll always end up with overspend into an ad type that doesn't actually perform that well on cold audiences let's talk about what in media buying actually died what doesn't matter anymore and then what still matters because there's a lot of stuff that is irrelevant these days. And when I say media buying still matters, I'm talking about a very specific subset of things within the account. There's a lot of stuff that you can push to the side. What 99% of people shouldn't be doing is daily bid tweaks. Going into the account using cost caps or bid caps and just changing bids every single day. Now, that used to be a strategy four or five years ago that a lot of people did quite well with, but these days you're really moving the needle on a variable, on a lever that has nowhere near as much leverage as other things that you could be focusing on.
